accuracy.evidence: Every number fact in the lab, text and items was checked: one more than n is n+1 and one less is n-1 throughout, the staircase towers are exactly 1 to 6 cubes, the frog lands on 4, 7 and 10 from 3, 6 and 9, and the cup rounds give 7, 4 and 10. Standards quoted match CCSS K.CC.4c and the Year 1 number and place value objective 'given a number, identify one more and one less'.

misconceptions.evidence: Names the four documented early-counting slips and builds each into the lab: giving the same number back, giving the number before, jumping two, and recounting from 1 instead of counting on. The decade crossing (9 to 10, 19 to 20) is called out in the adult text and the frog's last hop lands on 10 on purpose.

lab_distinct.evidence: A new canvas lab written for this topic: a tower that grows by dragged cubes, a six-tower staircase built from a shuffled tray with too-tall and too-short feedback, a frog on a two-row 1 to 10 track, a bin for one less, and a cup that hides the count so the child must count on. It passed the 30% shingle gate against all other flag labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The order goes from seeing one more (one cube added, number spoken), to the pattern (each step of the staircase is one taller), to one more as a number-track move, to the inverse (one less), to counting on from a hidden total. Each step's success line names what the child just showed, so the idea is drawn out of the action rather than told first.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each tested by the step that follows: 5 and one more (choices 6, 5, 7), one more than 9 (10, 8, 9, aimed at the decade slip), 7 take one away (6, 8, 7), and whether to say 6 then 7 or count from 1 again before the hidden-cup rounds; the confirmation repeats the guess and says whether it held.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions (one more than 4, ducks 8 and one more, one less than 6, sweets in a bag to count on, just after 9, and one more than Mo's 3 cars), with wrong-answer messages tagged by slip: same number, the number before, jumped two, went up instead of down, counted again from 1, and a guess. Each says what the chosen answer really is.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short spoken sentences built on blocks, towers and the counting words themselves, within the family kid FK limit; the adult text is within its limit and uses the curriculum terms successor, cardinality, stable order and counting on with a plain gloss. Canvas headings stay under eight words and spoken lines repeat the number aloud.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler phrase scan and the 12% duplication gate. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (one more, the next number, one less, count on), the adult text covers standards, links to earlier counting skills, named mistakes and what the lab does, and the family tip is two quick home routines.

mobile.evidence: Checked on the iPhone 13 walkthrough and 390 px screenshots of every step before and after Show me: the 10-cube tower in One less was resized to fit above the answer cards, the 1 to 10 track wraps to two rows of five, the staircase tray keeps six columns, and the young class gives large buttons with at most ten number buttons.

accessibility.evidence: axe WCAG 2.1 AA was clean in light and dark themes on desktop and phone. Every drag has a labelled button twin (Add one cube, Tower of n, number buttons 1 to 10, Take one away, Drop one in), and the canvas aria-label is updated with each spoken line so a screen reader hears the current count.
